To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the cost-effectiveness of birth-cohort screening for hepatitis C (HCV) antibody was sensitive to the prevalence of HCV antibody, the proportion of HCV antibody-positive persons who were linked to care, and the proportion of persons who were HCV antibody-positive and who were treated, and (b) birth-cohort screening was cost-effective compared with no screening at a prevalence of HCV of 0.2% and above.

the incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) for the birth-cohort screening strategy for hepatitis C antibody in primary care ranged from $2,000 to $4,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained.
